title: Paper 2 comparative essay and the individual oral
summary: How to write a comparative essay on two literary works under exam conditions, and how to plan and deliver the 15-minute individual oral on a global issue.

keyterms.definition: A comparative essay on two literary works studied, answering one of four general questions in 1 h 45 min (30 marks).
The internal assessment: a 10-minute prepared response plus 5 minutes of teacher questions, on a global issue in two extracts.
A passage of up to about 40 lines chosen from a work or body of work for the individual oral.
A collection of non-literary texts by one author or creator, such as a series of adverts or a photographer's portfolio.
The single page of up to 10 bullet points you may bring into the individual oral.
Paper 2 criterion A (10 marks): knowledge of both works and interpretation relevant to the question.
Paper 2 criterion B (10 marks): analysis of authorial choices and comparison of how the works create meaning.
A Paper 2 question not tied to particular works, which you apply to two works you studied.
Phrases that tell the listener or reader where an argument is going, e.g. 'Turning now to the advert…'.
The complete text an extract comes from; the oral must connect the extract to it.

questions.prompt: Which texts can you write about in Paper 2?
options: Two literary works you studied in class
One non-literary body of work and one poem from the exam paper
questions.explanation: Paper 2 requires two literary works studied in the course, not the works used in your oral or HL essay.

questions.statement: Paper 2 is worth 35% at SL and 25% at HL.
questions.explanation: The paper is the same at both levels, but HL weighting is lower because HL also has the HL essay.

questions.text: Paper 2 questions are ___ questions, not tied to specific works.
questions.explanation: You must apply a general question about literature to two works you know well.

questions.prompt: Question: "How do two works you have studied present the tension between duty and desire?" What should your thesis do?
options: Make a comparative claim about how and why each work presents that tension
questions.explanation: A comparative thesis answers the question for both works and signals similarities and differences.

questions.prompt: Match each Paper 2 criterion to its focus and maximum mark.
questions.explanation: Criteria A and B carry most of the 30 marks, so knowledge and analysis are essential.

questions.statement: You can bring copies of your works into the Paper 2 exam.
questions.explanation: Paper 2 is closed-book, so learn key quotations and precise references.

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation for Paper 2?
options: Learn key quotations and practise applying both works to many different questions
questions.explanation: Flexible knowledge lets you shape material to whatever question appears.

questions.text: Paper 2 criterion B rewards analysis of authorial choices and how the works are ___.
questions.explanation: Comparison of how meaning is created must run through the essay.

questions.prompt: A Paper 2 paragraph discusses only one work. What is the main risk?
options: It weakens comparison, which is central to the task
questions.explanation: Some single-work focus is fine, but each paragraph should feed a comparative argument.

questions.prompt: Order the first 15 minutes of Paper 2.
items: Choose the question that best fits your two works
Write a comparative thesis and paragraph plan
questions.explanation: Choosing carefully and planning comparatively saves time later.

questions.prompt: What does the individual oral consist of?
options: 10 minutes of prepared response and 5 minutes of teacher questions
questions.explanation: Fifteen minutes in total: a 10-minute response then 5 minutes of questions.

questions.text: In the oral, one text is a literary work and the other is a non-literary ___ of work.
questions.explanation: A body of work is a collection of non-literary texts by the same creator.

questions.statement: You may bring an outline of up to 10 bullet points into the oral.
questions.explanation: The outline supports memory but must not be a script.

questions.prompt: Approximately how long may each extract be?
questions.explanation: Short extracts allow close analysis within 10 minutes.

questions.prompt: Match the oral criterion to its focus.
questions.explanation: Each oral criterion is worth 10 marks, giving 40.

questions.statement: It is enough to discuss only the two extracts without mentioning the works they come from.
questions.explanation: You must connect each extract to its whole work or body of work.

questions.prompt: Which opening best sets up an oral?
options: Today I will talk about two texts.
My global issue is how economic pressure erodes family bonds, explored through a domestic drama and a bank's advertising campaign.
I like these texts a lot.
First, the author was born in 1960.
questions.explanation: It states a precise global issue and names both texts and their roles.

questions.text: Phrases like "Moving now to the campaign…" that guide the listener are called ___.
questions.explanation: Signposting helps with focus and organization in spoken work.

questions.prompt: How should time be divided between the two texts?
options: All on the non-literary body of work
questions.explanation: Balance is part of focus and organization; both texts must be analysed.

items: Introduce the global issue and both texts
Analyse the first extract and link to its whole work
Analyse the second extract and link to its body of work
Conclude by drawing the texts together
questions.explanation: A clear arc supports a coherent response; some students integrate both texts throughout instead.
